items.title: Level 2: Reading the advert before you prepare
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Your best preparation tool is the job advert on Civil Service Jobs. It is not just a description of the job. It tells you how you will be assessed. Look for the section that says how the selection process will work. It will list the stages, which may include an online application, a sift, a test and an interview. A sift is the first check of the applications, where a team decides who goes through to the next stage. The advert will also name the behaviours, and sometimes the strengths, that will be tested at interview. Write these in a list and keep it beside you. Next, read the 'responsibilities' or 'duties' part. For an Administrative Officer role, these are often things like answering enquiries, keeping records up to date, processing paperwork, using IT systems and working as part of a team. For each duty, think of a time you have done something similar, even if it was not in paid work. Answering a phone at a club, keeping accounts for a sports team or helping a relative with their post all count as relevant experience. Also look at the closing date, the location and the grade. The grade for this level of job is usually called AO, short for Administrative Officer. Finally, check for words such as 'essential' and 'desirable', which show what the department treats as a must-have and what is a bonus. Keep a copy of the advert, because the page can disappear once the vacancy closes.

questions.prompt: Why is the job advert the best preparation tool?

options.text: It shows how you will be assessed and which behaviours matter
It names the panel members who will be scoring your answers
It explains which of the other applicants you are competing with
It lists the questions that the panel has chosen for the day

questions.hint: The advert names the stages and the behaviours that will be tested.

questions.prompt: What is a 'sift' in Civil Service recruitment?

options.text: The final stage where the top candidates are ranked for offers
A list of candidates who have been offered the job already
A written test taken at the start of the interview day
The first check of applications to decide who goes through

questions.hint: A sift is when applications are reviewed and shortlisted.

questions.prompt: Which part of the advert tells you what you may be asked about at interview?

options.text: The paragraph describing the department's history
The section giving the location and the closing date
The notes about how to claim travel expenses
The list of behaviours and strengths to be assessed

questions.hint: The advert lists the behaviours and strengths being tested.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful thing to do with the list of duties in the advert?

options.text: Rank the duties by how senior the people doing them are
Copy the duties into your answers in the advert's own words
Match each duty to a time you did something similar
Pick the duties you have never done and avoid them

questions.hint: Duties show you what kinds of example to prepare.

questions.prompt: Which of these could count as relevant experience for an AO role?

options.text: Knowing a family friend who works in the Civil Service
Watching television programmes about office life
Reading a lot about how government departments work
Keeping the accounts for a local sports team

questions.hint: Unpaid work such as club accounts is relevant experience.

questions.prompt: What does 'AO' stand for in a Civil Service job title?

options.text: Assistant Office Organiser
Administrative Officer
Assistant Operations Officer
Administrative Operator

questions.hint: AO is the grade name for Administrative Officer.

questions.prompt: How does a 'desirable' requirement differ from an 'essential' one?

options.text: Desirable is tested at sift, while essential is tested at interview
Desirable is a bonus, while essential is a must-have
Desirable is for managers, while essential is for new starters
Desirable is tested on paper, while essential is tested in person

questions.hint: Essential means you must show it, and desirable is a bonus.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep a copy of the advert?

options.text: Panels expect you to quote it back to them in the interview
It is needed as proof when you claim travel expenses
You must return a signed copy when you accept an offer
The advert can disappear once the vacancy closes

questions.hint: Adverts are taken down after the closing date.

questions.prompt: Which task is a typical duty for an Administrative Officer?

options.text: Leading a team of experienced staff
Keeping records up to date
Managing the budget for a whole team
Writing detailed policy advice for ministers

questions.hint: AO duties often include records, enquiries and paperwork.

questions.prompt: What does the closing date on the advert tell you?

options.text: The day on which the interviews will be held
The last day on which applications are accepted
The date you would start work if successful
The day your invitation will be sent out

questions.hint: The closing date is the application deadline.

items.title: Level 2: Why panels ask about the past
items.body: Most Civil Service interviews use behaviour-based questions. These usually start with 'Tell us about a time when you...' or 'Give an example of...'. The idea behind them is simple: the best clue to how you will act in future is how you have acted in the past. Rather than asking 'Are you a good team member?', which anyone can say yes to, the panel asks for a real story. Then they can judge what you did and how well it worked. This is also fairer, because it focuses on evidence, not on who talks the best. Behaviour-based questions are linked to the behaviours in the advert. For example, a question about Working Together might be 'Tell us about a time you helped a colleague who was struggling.' A question about Delivering at Pace might be 'Describe a time you had to meet a tight deadline.' You can answer with an example from any part of your life, as long as it is real and you played a part. Panels often use follow-up questions to dig into the detail, such as 'What did you say to them?' or 'What would you do differently?' This is why you must choose examples you remember well. If you invent or exaggerate, a few follow-up questions will show it. Choose a story where the action you took was your own choice and the result was clear. Small, ordinary examples are fine, as long as they show the behaviour clearly.

questions.prompt: What is the idea behind behaviour-based questions?

options.text: Answers about general knowledge are easier to compare fairly
People who plan carefully for the future always perform best
A candidate's qualifications show how well they will do the job
Past behaviour is a good clue to how you will act in future

questions.hint: The best clue to future behaviour is what you did before.

questions.prompt: Which phrase usually begins a behaviour-based question?

options.text: 'Where do you see yourself in five years...'
'Tell us about a time when you...'
'How would you describe yourself in three words...'
'What would you do if you were the manager...'

questions.hint: Behaviour questions ask for a real past example.

questions.prompt: Why is asking for a real story more useful than asking 'Are you a good team member?'

options.text: A story shows that you have the right qualifications
A claim is harder to remember than a story from the past
A story takes less time for the panel to score than a claim
Anyone can claim to be one, but a story gives evidence

questions.hint: Evidence is more reliable than a bare claim.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour might a question about meeting a tight deadline test?

options.text: Seeing the Big Picture
Making Effective Decisions
Managing a Quality Service
Delivering at Pace

questions.hint: Deadlines relate to Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: Which behaviour might the question 'Tell us about a time you helped a struggling colleague' test?

options.text: Making Effective Decisions
Managing a Quality Service
Seeing the Big Picture
Working Together

questions.hint: Supporting a colleague is Working Together.

questions.prompt: Where can your examples come from?

options.text: Only study or training done for a qualification
Any part of your life, provided they are real
Only experience gained during the past twelve months
Only paid work done in an office or similar workplace

questions.hint: Real examples can come from work, study, volunteering or home.

questions.prompt: Why do panels ask follow-up questions?

options.text: To test how well you cope with being interrupted
To check the detail and what you personally did
To move the interview on to the next behaviour sooner
To give you a second chance to repeat your first answer

questions.hint: Follow-ups test the depth of your example.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of inventing or exaggerating an example?

options.text: You will run out of time before reaching the result
Invented examples cannot be told in STAR order
Follow-up questions can quickly show that it is false
Examples must be checked with your referee before scoring

questions.hint: A few follow-up questions can show up an invented story.

questions.prompt: Which example is most likely to work well?

options.text: A small everyday story where your action and result are clear
A long story with lots of background about the people
A recent news event that you felt strongly about
A dramatic story in which the whole team shared the credit

questions.hint: A clear personal action and result is what the panel wants.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to choose an example you remember well?

options.text: Panels may ask for more detail about it
The panel will check it against your application word for word
You will be asked to write it up after the interview
You will be asked to tell it twice to two panel members

questions.hint: Detail questions are easy if you remember the story.

questions.prompt: What does a good answer to 'Tell us about a time you made a mistake' show?

options.text: That you can own an error and learn from it
That you work more slowly to avoid mistakes
That you can explain why the mistake was unavoidable
That you can put mistakes right before anyone notices

questions.hint: Panels want honesty and learning.

items.title: Level 2: Choosing and sorting your examples
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: A good way to prepare is to build a small bank of examples. Aim for five or six strong stories rather than twenty weak ones. Each story should be something you did, with a clear result, and it should be able to cover more than one behaviour. For example, a time you helped a new colleague settle in could show Working Together and also Developing Self and Others. A time you handled a queue of customers could show Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service. Write each example as a few bullet notes, not a script: the situation in one line, the task in one line, three or four actions, and the result. Use a mix of sources. If every example comes from the same job, the panel may feel your experience is narrow. If you have little paid work, use college, volunteering, caring, sports clubs, a community group or helping a neighbour. Panels are interested in the behaviour, not the setting. Do not use the same example for two questions in the same interview unless the panel has asked you for something very different, because it looks as if you have little to offer. If you only have one example for a behaviour, consider whether you can use a different part of it. Practise saying each story aloud in two minutes. Time yourself. Short bullet notes help you remember the key points without sounding rehearsed.

questions.prompt: How many examples is it sensible to build into your bank?

options.text: One flexible one for every question
About twenty short ones
Five or six strong ones
Two, one for each panel member

questions.hint: A small bank of strong examples is easier to remember.

questions.prompt: Why might one example cover more than one behaviour?

options.text: The panel marks only the first behaviour in a story
Behaviours are all the same thing under different names
One story can show several behaviours at once
The panel can mark a story twice for each behaviour

questions.hint: One story can show, for example, Working Together and Developing Self and Others.

questions.prompt: Which two behaviours might a story about helping a new colleague settle in show?

options.text: Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service
Making Effective Decisions and Changing and Improving
Working Together and Developing Self and Others
Leadership and Seeing the Big Picture

questions.hint: Helping a new colleague links to those two.

questions.prompt: A time you dealt with a queue of customers could best show which pair of behaviours?

options.text: Delivering at Pace and Managing a Quality Service
Developing Self and Others and Changing and Improving
Communicating and Influencing and Leadership
Seeing the Big Picture and Leadership

questions.hint: A queue involves both speed and service quality.

questions.prompt: How should you write down each example?

options.text: As a long essay covering every detail of the story
As short bullet notes you can glance at
As one sentence naming only the result
As a full script you can read out word for word

questions.hint: Bullet notes help you remember without sounding rehearsed.

questions.prompt: Why use a mix of sources for your examples?

options.text: Examples from different sources score higher by rule
Each behaviour must come from a different employer
Using one job only can make your experience seem narrow
Panels do not accept more than two examples from one job

questions.hint: A range shows breadth of experience.

questions.prompt: What can you use if you have little paid work?

options.text: Experiences of friends who have done similar jobs
Skills you plan to learn once you have the job
Volunteering, college, caring or a club
Imaginary situations that show how you would act

questions.hint: Panels care about the behaviour, not whether you were paid.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to use the same example for several questions?

options.text: The panel will be unable to score it a second time
You will run out of time halfway through
It can make you look as if you have little to offer
It is against the rules of the interview

questions.hint: Repeating suggests a narrow range of experience.

questions.prompt: How can you check that an example fits in the time?

options.text: Ask a friend to read it and say if it seems long
Read it silently once and check that it fits on a page
Say it aloud and time yourself to about two minutes
Count the words and aim for about two hundred of them

questions.hint: Timing a spoken version is the most reliable check.

questions.prompt: What matters most to a panel about the setting of an example?

options.text: That it involved a large budget or many people
The behaviour it shows, not where it happened
That it happened in an office or similar workplace
That it took place within the last twelve months

questions.hint: Panels look at the behaviour, not the setting.

questions.prompt: What should the Action part of your notes list?

options.text: The names of everyone involved at the time
A summary of what the team achieved overall
Three or four specific things you did, in order
An explanation of why the organisation needed the work

questions.hint: Action shows your own steps.

items.title: Level 2: How the panel scores you
items.body: Civil Service interviews are scored, so that decisions are fair and based on evidence. Each panel member usually writes down what you say and then gives a score for each behaviour or strength. Many Civil Service interviews use a numbered scale, such as 1 to 7, where a low number means little or no evidence and a high number means strong, clear evidence. The exact scale and the pass mark can differ between departments, and the advert or the recruitment team will explain the scoring if it matters for your job. The score depends on the evidence you give, not on how confident you sound or how well you speak. A short answer with a clear action and result can score better than a long, rambling one. The panel looks for evidence of what you did, what the result was and how well your actions fit the behaviour. They also notice if you describe only what the team did, because they cannot score you for that. After the interviews, the panel compares scores and may talk through any differences. Candidates are then ranked, and the highest-scoring people who meet the pass mark are offered the jobs. In some cases a candidate who passes but is not at the top is placed on a reserve list. The panel does not score you on your accent, your appearance or your background. They score you against the same criteria as everyone else.

questions.prompt: Why are Civil Service interviews scored?

options.text: So the panel can finish more quickly than usual
So decisions are fair and based on evidence
So every candidate ends with the same total
So candidates can compare themselves with each other

questions.hint: Scoring supports fair, evidence-based decisions.

questions.prompt: What does a high number on a 1 to 7 scale usually show?

options.text: That the panel liked you personally the most
Strong, clear evidence for the behaviour
That your answer was longer than the others
That you spoke more quickly than other candidates

questions.hint: A higher score means stronger evidence.

questions.prompt: How consistent is the scoring scale and pass mark across departments?

options.text: They are identical in every department and agency
They are the same except for senior grades
They can differ, so check the advert or ask
They are set by each panel on the day

questions.hint: The scale and pass mark can vary.

questions.prompt: What does the score mainly depend on?

options.text: The evidence you give of what you did
How long your answers last compared with others
How confident and polished you appear
How closely your answers match other candidates

questions.hint: Scores follow evidence, not style alone.

questions.prompt: Which answer is likely to score better?

options.text: A confident answer that gives no detail
A long answer that covers several different topics
An answer that describes what the team did overall
A short answer with a clear action and result

questions.hint: Clear evidence beats length.

questions.prompt: Why can describing only what 'the team' did cost you marks?

options.text: Teamwork is not assessed at Administrative Officer level
The panel can only score what you personally did
Panels mark down any mention of colleagues
It makes the answer shorter than the minimum time

questions.hint: The panel scores your own actions.

questions.prompt: What happens after the interviews finish?

options.text: Panels compare scores and candidates are ranked
Candidates are asked to rate how well they think they did
Everyone interviewed is told their score straight away
The panel picks the candidate it liked most overall

questions.hint: Ranking is based on scores.

questions.prompt: What does a place on a reserve list usually mean?

options.text: You were rejected but may appeal the decision
You passed but were not top of the ranking
You were offered the job but turned it down
You were interviewed but your answers were not scored

questions.hint: It means you could be offered a similar job later.

questions.prompt: Which of these should a fair panel NOT use when scoring you?

options.text: The action you personally took
Your accent or background
How well the example fits the behaviour
The result you describe in your example

questions.hint: Panels score evidence against criteria, not personal background.

questions.prompt: Who sets the criteria the panel scores against?

options.text: They change from candidate to candidate by experience
They are chosen by the panel after seeing the candidates
They are set in advance in the advert and assessment plan
They are agreed by the panel once interviews finish

questions.hint: Criteria are set in advance and published in the advert.

questions.prompt: Why might panel members compare scores after the interviews?

options.text: To decide which member scored most accurately
To make sure each member gave an identical score
To check consistency and discuss any differences
To remove the highest and lowest scores from the totals

questions.hint: Comparing scores supports fair and consistent decisions.

items.title: Level 2: Behaviours compared with strengths
items.body: A Civil Service interview may test behaviours, strengths or both. They are different, and it helps to know how. Behaviour questions ask what you have done. You give a real past example and the panel scores what you did. They need preparation: you choose your stories, practise them and keep notes. Strengths questions are about what you enjoy and what comes naturally to you. They are asked quickly, often with only a short time to think, and answers are short. There is no example to prepare. Instead you prepare by knowing yourself. Strengths-based interviews are built on the idea that people do their best work when they are doing what they enjoy, so the panel is watching for energy, such as a lift in your voice or a smile when you talk about something you love. A strengths question might be 'What would you do with a free day?' or 'Do you prefer to start tasks or finish them?' A behaviour question might be 'Tell us about a time you had to deal with an angry customer.' Some interviews mix both types. If so, the invitation or advert usually tells you which of the types to expect. For behaviour questions use STAR. For strengths questions answer honestly and briefly, say why you enjoy it and, if you can, give a quick example. Do not treat strengths questions as a trap. Being yourself is the best preparation.

questions.prompt: How do behaviour questions differ from strengths questions?

options.text: One asks for past evidence, the other about what energises you
One is for managers and the other is for new starters
One is scored and the other is only for conversation
One is spoken and the other is answered in writing

questions.hint: Behaviour asks what you did, and strengths asks what you enjoy.

questions.prompt: How are strengths questions usually paced?

options.text: Slowly, with each answer lasting several minutes
In writing, with time to plan each answer
With the panel giving a list of topics in advance
Quickly, with short answers expected

questions.hint: Strengths questions are quick and short.

questions.prompt: What are strengths-based panels watching for?

options.text: A fluent recital of a prepared answer
Energy and natural enthusiasm
Detail about what the team achieved
Formal vocabulary and precise grammar

questions.hint: Panels notice natural energy.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a strengths question?

options.text: Do you prefer to start tasks or finish them?
Give an example of working with a colleague you disagreed with.
Tell us about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.
Describe a situation where you met a tight deadline.

questions.hint: This asks about preference, not past evidence.

questions.prompt: Which question below asks for a real example from your past?

options.text: What gives you the most energy at work?
Tell us about a time you resolved a disagreement.
Would you rather work alone or in a team?
What would you do with a free day?

questions.hint: Behaviour questions ask for a real past example.

questions.prompt: What is the best way to prepare for strengths questions?

options.text: Think honestly about what you enjoy and do well
Write a script of one-line replies to the common ones
Memorise a polished answer for each likely question
Research which strengths the department values most

questions.hint: Self-awareness is the best preparation.

questions.prompt: Which method gives structure to an answer to a behaviour question?

options.text: STAR
SMART
PEST
SWOT

questions.hint: STAR gives behaviour answers a clear order.

questions.prompt: How can you find out which types of question to expect?

options.text: The job title shows which type will be used
The advert or invitation usually says
The department's website lists the questions
The panel decides on the day and tells you at the start

questions.hint: The advert or invitation usually states the types.

questions.prompt: Why are strengths questions hard to rehearse?

options.text: Panels forbid candidates from preparing any answers
The questions change depending on your first answer
Rehearsed answers lose the natural honesty panels want
There are too many possible questions to prepare for

questions.hint: Over-rehearsed answers sound false.

questions.prompt: How much time might you have to think about a strengths question?

options.text: As long as you ask for
Around two minutes, as for a behaviour question
Usually a full minute of silence
Often only a few seconds

questions.hint: Strengths questions are quick, so thinking time is short.

items.title: Level 2: Setting up for a video interview
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: If your interview is by video, treat it as seriously as one in an office. Begin with the technology. Find out from the invitation which platform is used, such as Microsoft Teams or Zoom, and whether you need to install an app or can use a web browser. Do this a few days before, not on the morning. Join a test call, and check that you can see and hear clearly. Use a laptop or computer if you can, as a phone screen is small and easy to knock. If you do use a phone, prop it up so that it does not move. Plug in your device or make sure the battery is full, and use headphones if the room is noisy. Check your Wi-Fi in the room you will use. If it is weak, sit closer to the router or use a cable. Tidy the space behind you or choose a plain wall, and check that nothing embarrassing or distracting is in view. Look at the position of your camera. It should be at eye level, with your head and shoulders visible, so you may need to put your laptop on a pile of books. Dress smartly from top to bottom, as you might have to stand. During the interview, sit up, smile when appropriate, and look at the camera when you speak. Nod to show you are listening. If the sound cuts out, say so calmly. Do not pretend you heard.

questions.prompt: Where do you find out which video platform will be used?

options.text: On the department's main website
On the screen at the start of the call
In the invitation email or message
In a message the panel sends once you are in the call

questions.hint: The invitation names the platform.

questions.prompt: When should you test the video technology?

options.text: A few days before, so there is time to fix problems
On the morning of the interview, once you are dressed
During the first few minutes of the interview
Only if the invitation says a test is needed

questions.hint: Testing early gives time to fix any problem.

questions.prompt: Why is a laptop usually better than a phone for a video interview?

options.text: A laptop camera always has better lighting
Panels give extra credit to candidates using laptops
A phone cannot join calls on the platforms used
A laptop screen is larger and steadier than a phone

questions.hint: A bigger, steadier screen helps.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible step to take with your device's power?

options.text: Keep it in low-power mode to save battery
Switch it off first so the battery rests
Charge it only after the interview begins
Plug it in, or make sure the battery is full

questions.hint: A flat battery would end the interview.

questions.prompt: What can you do if your Wi-Fi is weak where you will sit?

options.text: Move to a busy cafe where the signal is strong
Sit near the router or use a cable
Turn off your camera to save bandwidth
Ask the panel to call you by phone instead

questions.hint: Test and fix the connection beforehand.

questions.prompt: How should your camera be positioned?

options.text: Slightly below your chin, showing your whole upper body
High above you, so the room behind is visible
Close to your face, so your expression is clear
At eye level, showing your head and shoulders

questions.hint: Eye level looks natural and professional.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible approach to clothes for a video interview?

options.text: Dress as you would for an interview in an office
Choose bright patterned clothes so you stand out
Dress smartly only from the waist up, since only that shows
Dress casually, as the panel cannot see you properly

questions.hint: Dressing fully avoids awkward moments.

questions.prompt: Where should you look when you speak on a video call?

options.text: At your own picture, to check how you look
At the panel's faces, so you can read their reactions
At the corner of the screen where the panel sit
At the camera lens, which feels like eye contact

questions.hint: The camera lens is where the panel feels you are looking.

questions.prompt: If the sound cuts out but the picture stays, what is the best response?

options.text: Say so calmly and ask for the question again
Carry on and give your best guess at the question
Switch to a different device without telling the panel
Turn off your camera until the problem passes

questions.hint: Honesty keeps the interview fair.

questions.prompt: Why can small nods and smiles help on video?

options.text: They replace the need to answer every question aloud
They hide delays caused by a slow connection
They show you are listening without speaking over anyone
They tell the panel that your answer has finished

questions.hint: Small gestures show engagement.

questions.prompt: What should you do about the background behind you?

options.text: Leave the room as it is, because the panel will not look
Choose a plain, tidy space or a plain wall
Use a busy picture so you seem relaxed
Show your bookshelf so the panel learn about you

questions.hint: A plain background keeps attention on you.

items.title: Level 2: Listening and structuring your answer
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: A well-structured answer is easier for the panel to score. The first skill is listening. Hear the whole question, and notice the key words. If the question is 'Tell us about a time you had to explain something complicated to someone', the key words are 'explain' and 'complicated'. Your example needs to match them. If you are given a moment, jot down a few words. Then choose your example, take a breath and begin. Use the STAR order. Start with a very short Situation and Task, perhaps two sentences, so the panel knows where you were. Spend most of the time on Action, saying what you did, step by step, and why you did it. The 'why' shows your thinking. Finish with the Result, which should answer the question directly. A common mistake is to spend too long on the background and then rush the actions. Another is to say 'we' throughout. Try to say 'I decided', 'I explained', 'I checked'. Avoid filler such as 'sort of', 'basically' and 'you know'. Short pauses are better. Keep to one example per question unless the panel asks for another. If you finish early, it is fine to stop. If you notice you are rambling, you can finish with 'So the result was...' to bring it back. Your answer should hang together like a short story with a beginning, a middle and an end.

questions.prompt: Why should you notice the key words in a question?

options.text: Your example needs to match what is actually being asked
They show you how long your answer should be
They tell you which panel member will score you
The panel gives marks for repeating them back

questions.hint: Matching the key words keeps your answer relevant.

questions.prompt: How much of your answer should the Situation and Task take?

options.text: Only the Task, as the Situation is not needed
A full minute, so the panel understand the context
About half of the whole answer
Short, perhaps two sentences in all

questions.hint: Keep the background short so there is time for action.

questions.prompt: Where should you spend most of your time in a STAR answer?

options.text: On the Situation, explaining the background
On the Task, describing who gave it to you
On the Action, saying what you did
On the Result, listing what the team achieved

questions.hint: Action shows what you did and why.

questions.prompt: Why does explaining why you took an action help?

options.text: It proves the story has been prepared
It lets you avoid describing the final result
It shows your thinking and judgement
It makes your answer long enough to be scored

questions.hint: The 'why' reveals your decision-making.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common mistake in answers?

options.text: Finishing with a clear result
Pausing before you begin to answer
Using 'I' when describing what you did
Spending too long on the background

questions.hint: Too much background leaves too little time for action.

questions.prompt: Which sentence shows your personal action best?

options.text: 'Each form was checked before it went out.'
'It was decided that each form would be checked.'
'I decided to check each form before it went out.'
'We decided to check each form before it went out.'

questions.hint: Using 'I' with a specific action shows what you did.

questions.prompt: What do filler words such as 'basically' and 'you know' do?

options.text: They count as extra detail in the scoring
They help the panel follow your train of thought
They show you are speaking naturally and honestly
They make your answer less clear and less confident

questions.hint: Fillers distract from the content.

questions.prompt: What can you do if you notice you are rambling?

options.text: Move to a second example to make up for it
Bring it back by saying what the result was
Stop speaking and ask whether the panel wants more
Start the answer again from the beginning

questions.hint: Moving to the Result gets you back on track.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you finish an answer sooner than you expected?

options.text: Repeat your result to emphasise the main point
Ask whether there is a minimum length required
Stop, and wait for the next question
Keep adding detail until two minutes have passed

questions.hint: A clear answer does not need to fill the time.

questions.prompt: Why is a story with a beginning, middle and end helpful?

options.text: The panel can follow it and find the evidence
It makes the answer easy to memorise word for word
It means every candidate's answers sound alike
It lets you avoid mentioning the details of your role

questions.hint: A clear structure makes evidence easy to find.

items.title: Level 2: Dealing with nerves and blanking
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK interview guidance
items.body: Interview nerves are common, and the panel knows it. Some physical signs are shaky hands, a dry mouth, a quick heartbeat and a voice that goes quiet or high. These are caused by adrenaline, which is the body's response to a challenge. You can reduce them with simple steps. Before the interview, prepare well, because knowing your examples is the best cure for anxiety. On the day, eat something light, drink water, and avoid too much caffeine, which can make you jittery. Move around gently beforehand to release tension. Breathing slowly, in for four and out for six, calms the body. In the interview, speak a little slower than you want to, and pause between sentences. A glass of water on the table helps with a dry mouth. If you blank, which means your mind goes empty, do not rush to fill the silence. Say 'That is a good question. Could I take a moment to think?' Most panels are happy to wait ten or fifteen seconds. You can also ask them to repeat the question, which gives you time. If you still cannot find an example, you can say, 'I would like to give a different example', or describe what you would do in that situation. Move on afterwards. One weaker answer will not decide the result, and you can do better on the next question. Do not apologise repeatedly. A calm recovery shows resilience.

questions.prompt: What causes shaky hands and a quick heartbeat before an interview?

options.text: Adrenaline, the body's normal response to a challenge
A medical condition that needs treating
A reaction to the panel's tone of voice
A sign that you have not prepared enough

questions.hint: Adrenaline is a normal response.

questions.prompt: What is the most effective way of reducing interview anxiety?

options.text: Learning answers to every possible question by heart
Preparing your examples so you know them well
Avoiding thinking about the interview until the last minute
Telling yourself firmly not to feel nervous

questions.hint: Good preparation reduces anxiety.

questions.prompt: Why might you limit caffeine on the day of the interview?

options.text: It can make you feel jittery and more anxious
It lowers the pitch of your voice on a call
It slows your thinking, so you answer too slowly
It dries your throat so much that you cannot speak

questions.hint: Too much caffeine can add to shakiness.

questions.prompt: What does 'blanking' mean in an interview?

options.text: You answer a different question from the one asked
Your mind suddenly goes empty
You run out of time for your answer
You hear the question wrongly

questions.hint: Blanking is when you cannot think of anything to say.

questions.prompt: What is a good first response to blanking?

options.text: Ask to start the interview again
Fill the silence with whatever comes to mind
Ask politely for a moment to think
Apologise and say that you are very nervous

questions.hint: A short pause is accepted.

questions.prompt: How long are most panels willing to wait while you think?

options.text: Two or three seconds at most
Until the end of the time allowed
Up to two minutes before they move on
Ten or fifteen seconds is usually fine

questions.hint: A short pause is normal.

questions.prompt: What does asking for the question to be repeated give you?

options.text: A better score for politeness
A little extra time to think
A shorter interview overall
A different question from the panel

questions.hint: Repeating the question buys thinking time.

questions.prompt: If you cannot find an example, what can you do?

options.text: Ask the panel to skip it and not score it
Make up a story that fits the question
Explain what you would do in that situation, or offer another example
Say the question does not apply to you

questions.hint: Honest alternatives are better than invention.

questions.prompt: After a weaker answer, what is the best approach?

options.text: Move on calmly and give the next answer your best
Ask the panel to mark that question again
Go back to correct it after every later question
Apologise each time you feel it was weak

questions.hint: One weak answer will not decide the result.

questions.prompt: What does recovering calmly after a blank show the panel?

options.text: That you can cope with pressure
That the question was unfair
That you did not prepare well
That you prefer easier questions

questions.hint: Recovering calmly shows resilience.

questions.prompt: How can gentle movement before the interview help?

options.text: It helps you remember your examples
It gives you energy for a longer answer
It stops adrenaline altogether
It can release tension

questions.hint: Light movement eases tension.

items.title: Level 2: Opening questions and the Civil Service Code
items.body: Many interviews start with a gentle opening question. Common ones are 'Why do you want this job?', 'Why the Civil Service?' and 'What do you know about our department?'. These are not behaviour questions, so STAR is not needed. A good answer is short, honest and specific. Say what attracts you to the work: for example, helping the public, being part of an organisation that delivers services for everyone, or the chance to learn and grow. Link this to the job. If the role involves processing claims, you might say you like work where careful accuracy affects real people. Show that you have read about the department, such as what it does and who it serves, and mention one fact that you found interesting. Do not simply repeat the website word for word. The Civil Service also has a Civil Service Code, which sets out four core values: integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality. Integrity means putting the obligations of public service above your own interests. Honesty means being truthful and open. Objectivity means basing your advice and decisions on evidence. Impartiality means acting fairly and without bias, whatever the government of the day. Showing that you understand these values, and giving a simple example of fairness or honesty from your own life, can strengthen your answer. Avoid saying that you want the job only for the pay or the pension, as this does not show interest in the work itself.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common opening question?

options.text: 'Talk us through every job on your CV in order'
'What would you change about the Civil Service?'
'Describe a time you led a team through a crisis'
'Why do you want this job?' or 'Why the Civil Service?'

questions.hint: Opening questions explore your motivation.

questions.prompt: How should you shape an answer to 'Why do you want this job?'

options.text: With a long history of your career so far
In four full STAR parts with a result
With a list of the benefits the job offers you
Briefly and honestly, linking your reasons to the job

questions.hint: Opening questions need a short, honest, specific answer.

questions.prompt: What makes a strong answer to 'Why the Civil Service?'

options.text: A list of the benefits you expect to receive
A summary of the department's website
A comment on a recent political debate
A genuine reason tied to public service and this role

questions.hint: Genuine, job-specific motivation stands out.

questions.prompt: Why mention one fact you learned about the department?

options.text: It helps the panel to remember your name
It proves you can recite facts accurately
It shows you have taken the trouble to research it
It allows you to skip questions on the department

questions.hint: A specific fact shows real interest.

questions.prompt: How many core values does the Civil Service Code set out?

options.text: Four
Seven
Five
Three

questions.hint: The four are integrity, honesty, objectivity and impartiality.

questions.prompt: Which of these is one of the Civil Service Code's core values?

options.text: Objectivity
Loyalty
Ambition
Efficiency

questions.hint: Objectivity is one of the four values.

questions.prompt: What does the Code mean by 'impartiality'?

options.text: Giving each customer exactly what they ask for
Avoiding difficult decisions altogether
Agreeing with whatever ministers prefer
Serving the government of the day fairly, without bias

questions.hint: Impartial means fair and unbiased.

questions.prompt: Which core value is about basing advice and decisions on evidence?

options.text: Impartiality
Objectivity
Honesty
Integrity

questions.hint: Objectivity is about evidence.

questions.prompt: Which core value is about putting public service above your own interests?

options.text: Honesty
Impartiality
Objectivity
Integrity

questions.hint: Integrity is about putting the obligations of public service first.

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to say you want the job only for the pay or pension?

options.text: The panel cannot reply to anything about pay
It suggests you have too much experience
It does not show interest in the work itself
It breaks the rule against discussing pay

questions.hint: Interest in the work is what panels want to hear.

items.title: Level 2: Answering a question about teamwork and communication
items.body: Working Together and Communicating and Influencing are very common in Administrative Officer interviews. Working Together is about building positive relationships and supporting your colleagues. Panels look for evidence that you share information, offer help, respect different views and keep going when a team is under pressure. A good example might be covering a colleague's work when they were off sick, or helping a new member of a club find their feet. Communicating and Influencing is about explaining things clearly, listening to others and adjusting your style to suit the person. Evidence could include writing a clear email, handling a difficult phone call or explaining a process to someone who was confused. When you tell these stories, include what you said or wrote, and why you chose that approach. For example: 'I could see the customer was upset, so I let them finish, then I repeated back the problem to show I understood, and explained the next steps in plain words.' Listening is just as important as speaking, so show that you checked understanding. Panels also like to hear how you handled a disagreement politely. Say what the other person wanted, how you found common ground, and what happened next. Avoid blaming others or describing a conflict where you were simply right and they were wrong. The panel wants to see that you can work with people whose views differ from yours.

questions.prompt: What is Working Together about?

options.text: Building positive relationships and supporting colleagues
Making sure your own work is always finished first
Representing your team to senior managers
Setting targets for the team and deciding who does each task

questions.hint: Working Together focuses on co-operation.

questions.prompt: Which is a good example of Working Together?

options.text: Covering a colleague's work while they were off sick
Telling your manager when a colleague makes an error
Taking charge of a project to meet the deadline
Finishing your own tasks early and leaving on time

questions.hint: Helping a colleague shows teamwork.

questions.prompt: What is Communicating and Influencing about?

options.text: Persuading others to accept your view at all costs
Sending detailed emails to everyone involved
Speaking confidently in front of large groups
Explaining clearly, listening and adapting your style

questions.hint: The behaviour covers clear explanation and listening.

questions.prompt: Which is a good example of Communicating and Influencing?

options.text: Sending the same email to a whole team to save time
Explaining a process to someone who was confused
Staying quiet in meetings to avoid conflict
Handing out written rules for people to follow

questions.hint: Making a process clear to someone is a good example.

questions.prompt: Why should you say why you chose an approach?

options.text: It shows your thinking as well as your action
It makes the answer long enough to score fully
It lets you leave out the result
It proves the example was rehearsed

questions.hint: The reason shows judgement.

questions.prompt: Why is repeating back a customer's problem useful?

options.text: It makes the call last long enough to be useful
It shows you listened and checks you understood
It gives you time to look up the answer
It lets you take control of the conversation

questions.hint: Checking understanding is part of listening.

questions.prompt: How should you describe a disagreement in an answer?

options.text: Explain what they wanted and how you found common ground
Say how your manager settled it for both of you
Explain why your view was right and theirs was mistaken
Describe how you avoided the disagreement entirely

questions.hint: Panels want to see you work with different views.

questions.prompt: Why is blaming others a poor approach in an answer?

options.text: It breaks the STAR order of the answer
It does not show you can work with different views
It is against the Civil Service Code to mention others
It makes the answer too short to score

questions.hint: Blame suggests a poor working relationship.

questions.prompt: Which of these shows adjusting your style to the person?

options.text: Using plain words with someone who was confused
Writing longer emails to people who are senior
Using the same technical terms with everyone
Speaking faster to people who seem in a hurry

questions.hint: Adapting your language to the listener shows skill.

questions.prompt: What does listening show in a Communicating example?

options.text: That you waited quietly for your turn to speak
That you agreed with everything the person said
That you checked you understood before acting
That you let the other person decide

questions.hint: Listening is as important as speaking.

questions.prompt: What kind of detail makes a communication example stronger?

options.text: How long the message took you to write
Which software you used to send it
The job titles of everyone who received the message
What you said or wrote, and why you chose that wording

questions.hint: The panel scores what you did and why.

items.title: Level 2: Questions you can ask, and ending well
items.body: At the end of the interview, the panel will usually ask if you have any questions. This is not a test, but it is another chance to leave a good impression. Prepare two or three questions that you genuinely want answered. Good questions focus on the job, the team and development. For example: 'What does a typical week look like in this team?', 'How does the team support new starters in their first few weeks?' or 'What training would I receive?' You might also ask about how the team measures its success, or what the biggest challenge for the team is right now. Questions like these show that you are thinking about doing the job well. Avoid questions that you could answer by reading the advert, and avoid asking about pay, leave or flexible working unless the panel brings it up, since these are covered in the offer stage. Do not ask a question just to fill the time, and do not say 'No, I think you have covered everything' if you had planned something. If your first questions have been answered, say so and ask a related one. It is also fine to ask what the next steps are and when you will hear. Then close the interview politely. Thank the panel by name if you can, say that you enjoyed the discussion, and say that you look forward to hearing from them. On video, wait for the host to end the call and leave the meeting yourself rather than closing the laptop suddenly.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of the questions you ask at the end?

options.text: A way for the panel to adjust your score
A moment for the panel to finish their notes
A test of how quickly you can think of questions
Another chance to show real interest in the job

questions.hint: Questions are another chance to show interest.

questions.prompt: How many questions is it sensible to prepare?

options.text: Just one, so that the panel is not delayed
None, because the panel has said everything
Two or three that you really want answered
As many as you can to show enthusiasm

questions.hint: A few well-chosen questions are enough.

questions.prompt: Which question shows interest in the job?

options.text: What does a typical week look like in this team?
Is overtime paid at a higher rate than normal hours?
Could I work from home every day of the week?
How quickly could I be promoted to the next grade?

questions.hint: A question about the work shows interest.

questions.prompt: Which topic is better left until the offer stage?

options.text: How the team supports new starters
Pay, leave and flexible working
What training new starters receive
What the team's biggest challenge is

questions.hint: These are usually covered later.

questions.prompt: Why avoid asking questions the advert already answers?

options.text: The panel is not allowed to repeat information
It suggests you did not read the advert carefully
It uses up time that is needed for scoring
It shows you are over-confident about getting the job

questions.hint: Reading the advert is basic preparation.

questions.prompt: What can you do if the panel has already answered your questions?

options.text: Ask the same question again to check the answer
Say you have none and let the call end
Say so, and ask a related question
Ask a question about the panel's own careers

questions.hint: A related follow-up still shows interest.

questions.prompt: Which is a sensible question about next steps?

options.text: Which candidate do you think was strongest?
Could you tell me if I have the job?
When will we hear the outcome?
How did my score compare with others?

questions.hint: Asking about timing is practical.

questions.prompt: How should you close the interview?

options.text: Ask the panel to confirm that you will be offered the job
Say you have applied for other jobs too
Summarise your best points again in a final speech
Thank the panel and say you enjoyed the discussion

questions.hint: A polite thank you is a good ending.

questions.prompt: On video, how should you end the call?

options.text: Wait for the host to end the call, then leave
Switch off your camera and wait to be removed
Leave the meeting before the panel say goodbye
Close the laptop as soon as you finish speaking

questions.hint: A calm, polite end is best.

questions.prompt: What does asking about the team's biggest challenge show?

options.text: That you would like to avoid the hardest tasks
That you doubt whether the team is well run
That you are already thinking about doing the job well
That you want the panel to explain the advert again

questions.hint: It shows thoughtful interest.

questions.prompt: Why is it a good idea to write your questions down beforehand?

options.text: The panel expects to see them written down
You are scored on how well your questions are written
Nerves can make it hard to think of questions at the time
Written questions are not forgotten by the panel

questions.hint: Preparing helps you ask something useful.

items.title: Level 2: Fairness, adjustments and your rights
items.source: Civil Service Jobs and GOV.UK guidance
items.body: The Civil Service aims to run recruitment fairly. It follows the Civil Service Commission's Recruitment Principles, which say that selection must be on merit, on the basis of fair and open competition. Merit means that the person who is best able to do the job is chosen. Fair means that every candidate is judged against the same criteria. Open means that jobs are advertised so that people have a chance to apply. If you have a disability or a health condition, you can ask for reasonable adjustments. A reasonable adjustment is a change that removes a disadvantage, so you can show your true ability. Examples include extra time, a change in format, a quiet room, rest breaks, written questions or a support worker. Under the Equality Act 2010 an employer must make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. You can ask at the application stage or after an invitation. Use the contact details on Civil Service Jobs. Many departments also take part in the Disability Confident scheme, which includes the guaranteed interview scheme: if you apply under it and meet the minimum criteria, you will be invited to interview. You can also ask for a different date if it clashes with a religious festival or a medical appointment, and the recruitment team will normally try to help. You do not need to share personal details with the panel. The recruitment team shares only what is needed to arrange the adjustment.

questions.prompt: What do the Recruitment Principles require of selection?

options.text: That it favours people already working in government
That it is decided by the department's own managers
That it rewards those with the highest qualifications
That it is on merit, through fair and open competition

questions.hint: The Principles require merit and fair, open competition.

questions.prompt: What does 'merit' mean in recruitment?

options.text: The person best able to do the job is chosen
The person from the department is chosen
The person with the most qualifications is chosen
The person who applied first is chosen

questions.hint: Merit means choosing the best person for the job.

questions.prompt: What does 'open' competition mean?

options.text: Jobs are advertised so people have a chance to apply
Candidates may see each other's scores
Anyone can turn up on the day
Interviews can be watched by anyone who asks

questions.hint: Open means vacancies are advertised.

questions.prompt: What is a reasonable adjustment?

options.text: A change to the job advert after publication
An extra mark added for candidates with a condition
A change to the pass mark to help some candidates
A change that removes a disadvantage so you can show your ability

questions.hint: Adjustments remove barriers so you can show your ability.

questions.prompt: Which law requires employers to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people?

options.text: The Data Protection Act 2018
The Employment Rights Act 1996
The Equality Act 2010
The Freedom of Information Act 2000

questions.hint: The Equality Act 2010 is the relevant law.

questions.prompt: Where can you find contact details to request an adjustment?

options.text: On the home page of GOV.UK for jobs
In the Civil Service Jobs advert or invitation
From the interview panel on the day
From your current employer's HR team

questions.hint: The recruitment team's contact details are on Civil Service Jobs.

questions.prompt: What does the guaranteed interview scheme offer?

options.text: A shorter list of checks, if you disclose
A job offer, if you meet the minimum criteria
A higher score, if you declare your condition
An interview, if you meet the minimum criteria

questions.hint: The scheme guarantees an interview, not the job.

questions.prompt: What can you ask for if an interview clashes with a religious festival?

options.text: A place in the next recruitment round only
A different date, which the team will try to arrange
A different panel for the same date
A shorter interview on the original date

questions.hint: The recruitment team will normally try to help.

questions.prompt: Who usually sees the details of your adjustment request?

options.text: Only the people who need them to arrange it
Your current employer and your referees
Every member of the recruitment team
All the panel members and the other candidates

questions.hint: Only what is needed is shared.

questions.prompt: Why is it fair to ask all candidates the same core questions?

options.text: Questions can be reused for the next vacancy
The panel can save time on preparation
Candidates can share answers beforehand
Everyone is compared on the same evidence

questions.hint: The same questions make comparisons fair.

items.title: Level 2: After the interview and following up
items.body: When the interview ends, you may feel unsure how it went. That is common. Try to note down a few points soon afterwards, such as the questions you were asked, the examples you used and anything you would do differently. These notes are useful for any future interview. Then give the recruitment team time. They have to compare the scores of everyone who was interviewed, which may include many people across several days. Results can take from a few days to a few weeks. If the invitation gave a date for hearing back, wait until it has passed before you contact them. When you hear, there are three main outcomes. First, an offer. This is usually conditional, which means subject to pre-employment checks. Checks commonly include identity, right to work, references, and the Baseline Personnel Security Standard, which checks identity, nationality and immigration status, employment history and unspent criminal records. Second, a place on a reserve list, which means you passed but were not top of the ranking. Third, a rejection. If you are rejected, ask for feedback, which the recruitment team normally provides. Read it without taking it personally. Look for patterns, such as answers that were too short, or a lack of detail on your own actions. Use it to adjust your examples for the next application. Do not hand in your notice at your current job until the offer is unconditional. Finally, keep applying. Civil Service jobs are advertised regularly, and many successful staff were rejected before they succeeded.

questions.prompt: What is a good thing to do soon after the interview?

options.text: Write down which candidate you think was strongest
Phone the panel chair for an early indication
Note down the questions you were asked and your examples
Contact each panel member to ask how you did

questions.hint: Short notes help with future interviews.

questions.prompt: When is it sensible to chase for a result?

options.text: Every few days until somebody replies
After the date given in the invitation has passed
A day after the interview, to show enthusiasm
Never, as the team will always reply within a week

questions.hint: Wait until the stated date has passed.

questions.prompt: Which of these are commonly included in pre-employment checks?

options.text: An examination of your school exam papers
Identity, right to work and references
A medical test of physical fitness
A review of your social media history

questions.hint: These are standard pre-employment checks.

questions.prompt: Which of these does the Baseline Personnel Security Standard cover?

options.text: Medical history, health records and fitness for work
Political views, party membership and voting record
Credit history, debts and spending records
Identity, right to work and unspent criminal records

questions.hint: BPSS checks identity, right to work, employment history and unspent convictions.

questions.prompt: Why might a passed candidate be placed on a reserve list?

options.text: The candidate was rejected but may apply again after a year
There were more successful candidates than jobs
The candidate was not interviewed because of a shortage of panels
The candidate was offered the job but declined it

questions.hint: A reserve list holds passed candidates for later vacancies.

questions.prompt: What can you ask for if you are rejected?

options.text: Feedback
A different panel to see you again
A re-score of your answers by the panel
A place on the reserve list

questions.hint: Feedback helps you improve.

questions.prompt: What should you look for when you read feedback?

options.text: Signs that the panel was biased against you
Clues about who was successful instead of you
Patterns, such as a lack of detail about your own actions
Reasons the questions were set unfairly

questions.hint: Patterns help you improve.

questions.prompt: Why is it worth applying again after a rejection?

options.text: Jobs are advertised regularly, and feedback helps next time
Reapplicants receive extra marks for persistence
Old scores are carried forward to the next process
The department must offer a place on a second try

questions.hint: Many staff succeeded after earlier rejections.

questions.prompt: What is the safest time to give notice to your current employer?

options.text: When the reserve list is confirmed
When the conditional offer arrives
As soon as you pass the interview
Once the offer is unconditional

questions.hint: Wait until the offer is no longer conditional.

questions.prompt: How might you view a result that is a rejection?

options.text: As evidence that you should not apply to government
As proof that the panel preferred internal staff
As feedback you can use, not a verdict on you
As a sign that you need a higher qualification

questions.hint: Rejection is common and feedback helps you improve.
